summary: Children aged 6-8 learn to interpret categorical data by using an organised display (their own pictogram, block diagram, or frequency table) to answer a ladder of questions: how many in one category, how many altogether across all categories, and the harder 'how many more/fewer' comparison. The central hurdle is that 'how many more' asks for a DIFFERENCE, not the larger category's value. Activities pose real questions about the child's own survey, model matching/subtracting for comparisons, and keep the running total reconciling with the whole group.
misconceptions: Answers 'how many more' with the larger category's value instead of the difference
Finds the total by counting the number of categories rather than summing the frequencies
Reads the wrong value by misaligning a row/column or miscounting
Treats each question in isolation, never checking the total against the whole group

activities.title: Question ladder on your own pets chart
steps: Collect a small survey (e.g. favourite pet) from your class or family and build it into a pictogram or block diagram.
Answer single-category questions first: 'How many children chose rabbits?' by reading the one row/column.
Answer a total question: 'How many children are there altogether?' by summing ALL the category frequencies, not counting how many kinds of pet there are.
Check your total against the number of people actually surveyed as a self-check.
Answer a comparison question: 'How many more chose dogs than cats?' by finding the difference.
Each time you give a comparison answer, say out loud how you got it.
activities.insight: Reading a single value, totalling all values, and comparing two values are three different moves; the total must reconcile with the whole group, and a comparison asks for a gap between two values.

activities.title: Line them up to see the difference
steps: Pick two categories to compare, e.g. dogs and cats.
Line the two rows up one-to-one so matching items sit directly beside each other.
Count the unmatched part that sticks out on the taller row — that is 'how many more'.
Confirm the same answer by subtracting: taller count minus shorter count (e.g. 8 dogs − 5 cats = 3).
Say the result in comparison words: 'There are 3 more dogs than cats' and 'there are 3 fewer cats than dogs.'
activities.insight: 'How many more' is the gap between the two categories — the unmatched part — not the height or count of the bigger one.

activities.title: Interactive chart with a comparison tool (optional scaffold)
steps: Open or build an interactive chart with a question panel under your survey data.
Tap one category and watch its bar light up to answer a single-value question.
Tap two categories (e.g. 'cats' and 'dogs') so the bars glide side by side and the extra squares on the taller bar are shaded as the answer to 'how many more'.
Press a total button that sums the categories and checks the sum equals the number of children surveyed.
After using the tool, redo one comparison and one total by hand to show you can do it without the highlighting.
activities.insight: Sliding two bars together and shading only the extra squares shows that 'how many more' is the highlighted gap, not the height of the bigger bar; a total button can reconcile the sum with the group size.

activities.title: Combine and reconcile checks
steps: Answer 'if the rabbit and cat groups joined, how many would that be?' by adding the two category counts.
Answer 'does your total match how many people you actually surveyed?' and, if not, recount.
Explain why, when each person surveyed gave exactly one answer, the total of all categories should equal the number of people surveyed.
activities.insight: Categories can be combined by adding their counts, and the sum of all categories should reconcile with the whole surveyed group — a built-in check on your reading.

checkQuestion: Here is our finished pets chart. Answer these for me: how many children chose rabbits? How many children are there altogether? And how many more chose dogs than cats? (Set the questions and WATCH how each answer is reached.)
checkAnswer: A correct performance: reads each category value correctly off the display, totals by summing ALL the frequencies (matching the number of children), and answers 'how many more' by finding the difference between the two categories (e.g. 8 dogs − 5 cats = 3), using comparison language.
